spec.description: A troubleshooting dashboard for the Kubernetes API server, written for someone new to it. The top answers 'what are clients seeing?' (refused, failed, timed out, slow, no answer) and on which kind of request; one tab per symptom then walks through the usual checks in order and ends with the CloudWatch Logs Insights query that names the caller. Prepared by Shane Corbett · Kubernetes Specialist (shancor@amazon.com). Please retain author attribution when sharing or adapting this dashboard.

spec.title: Webhook calls, rejections and fail-open, by webhook
spec.description:
Per webhook: how often it was called, how often the request was rejected (the policy saying no, or a failed call under failurePolicy Fail), and how often the server proceeded without its answer (fail-open: the call failed by timeout, connection error or webhook error, and failurePolicy Ignore skipped it).

**Healthy:** calls tracking the write rate, rejections you recognise, no fail-open at all.

**If not:** Any fail-open is serious. The name is the owner; the usual cause is the webhook's pods being down or too slow (the outbound failures chart shows the host).

spec.title: Each webhook's time per call right now (slowest 1 %)
spec.description:
One bar per admission webhook: how long a call to it takes, the slowest 1 %, read at the end of the range. Green under the 0.5 s mark, yellow over it, red at 1 s.

**Healthy:** every bar green and short. The webhook's name is its owner.

**If not:** A long bar is a webhook adding that much to every write it covers; the 504 tab's webhook time chart says since when.

defaults.noValue: no admission webhooks on this cluster

spec.title: Calls the server made to webhooks that failed, by host
spec.description:
The API server is a client too: admission webhook calls go out through its REST client, and this counts the ones that got a 5xx or no answer at all, by the host they went to. Calls to add-on APIs go through the aggregator instead and are not counted here; they show as 502 and 503 on the 5xx tab.

**Healthy:** none.

**If not:** The host names the webhook or add-on API; its own pods and logs take it from here. This is the cause behind a fail-open or a 500 `failed calling webhook`.

spec.title: Admission as a whole: mutate step and validate step (99 in 100 under)
spec.description:
Admission runs in two steps: first everything that may change the object (mutate), then everything that may refuse it (validate). This is the time of each whole step, all webhooks and built-in checks together.

**Healthy:** both steps under the dashed 0.5 s mark.

**If not:** A step high: the per-webhook chart says which webhook.

spec.title: Webhook fail-open, in the range
spec.description:
How many times the server proceeded with a write without a webhook's answer because the call failed (timeout, connection error or an error from the webhook) and its failurePolicy is Ignore. Each one is a rule silently skipped. The counter does not exist until the first event, so a cluster that has never failed open reads 'none in this range'.

**Healthy:** none in this range, or 0.

**If not:** Any: the calls chart names the webhook; its pods are down or too slow.

spec.title: Writes refused by a webhook, in the range
spec.description:
How many writes a webhook rejected, or failed against under failurePolicy Fail (the server counts both as rejected). Mostly the policy working as intended; a sudden rise still deserves a look.

**Healthy:** a number you recognise for this cluster's policies.

spec.title: Consistent reads the cache could not answer and sent to the database
spec.description:
Consistent reads (reads with no resourceVersion, which must be as fresh as the database) per second, by whether the cache answered them (fallback=false) or the server had to go to the database instead (fallback=true). Each fallback is a database call the cache was supposed to save.

**Healthy:** fallback=false, success=true, for every resource.

**If not:** fallback=true climbing: the cache is not keeping up (the wait chart beside this) and the database is carrying reads it should not; the database tab will show it.

Empty on an older control plane: that Kubernetes version does not export this metric. That says nothing about the cluster.

spec.title: Streaming LIST: time to send a whole collection (99 in 100 under), by resource
spec.description:
Newer clients can ask for a collection as a stream instead of one big response, which is far cheaper for the server. This is how long streaming a whole collection took, by resource.

**Healthy:** under the dashed 15 s mark. Empty is fine: no client on this cluster uses streaming LIST yet.

Empty on an older control plane: that Kubernetes version does not export this metric. That says nothing about the cluster.

spec.title: One stream in from the database, thousands out to watchers (log scale)
spec.description:
The server keeps a copy of everything in memory (the watch cache). One stream of changes comes in from the database; every change is sent on to every client watching that resource. Log scale, so the vertical gap is the fan-out.

**Healthy:** a steady gap; its size is just how many watchers the cluster has.

**If not:** Events out rising while watches stay flat: something is changing objects fast (status updates, leases). Events out rising with watches: a controller scaled out and every replica watches the same thing.

spec.title: Time a read waited for the cache to catch up (99 in 100 under), by resource
spec.description:
A read served from the cache must first be sure the cache is up to date with the database. This is how long that check took.

**Healthy:** milliseconds: the cache is at most a few changes behind.

**If not:** One resource waiting: its stream of changes is slow, which can be because its objects are large. Every resource waiting: the database is slow to deliver changes; see the database tab.

Empty on an older control plane: that Kubernetes version does not export this metric. That says nothing about the cluster.

spec.title: Watchers the server dropped, and whole collections it re-sent
spec.description:
The server drops a watcher that cannot keep up (a slow client). A new or re-connecting watcher gets the whole collection sent again first. Drops followed by re-sends is a client in a reconnect loop, re-reading everything each time.

**Healthy:** no drops; re-sends only when a controller restarts.

**If not:** A reconnect loop on a large resource is the classic self-inflicted LIST storm: the fairness tab shows which flow is paying for it, the slow tab's log query names the client.

spec.title: Consistent reads the cache could not answer
spec.description:
The share of consistent reads (reads with no resourceVersion, which must be as fresh as the database) the in-memory cache could not answer and had to pass to the database. Each one is a database call the cache was meant to save. The fallback series only appears after the first fallback, so a cache that has never fallen back reads 0 % as long as it reports reads at all.

**Healthy:** under 1 %.

**If not:** Rising: the cache is not keeping up with changes; the read-wait chart below says on which resource.

spec.title: Fan-out: events out per change in
spec.description:
For each change that came in from the database, how many watch events the server sent out. This is the multiplier the control plane pays for every change.

**Healthy:** steady over weeks. It grows when controllers scale out.

spec.title: Watch streams open
spec.description:
How many clients are watching for changes right now. Every change the server sees is sent to each watcher of that resource.

**Healthy:** roughly the number of controllers and nodes you have, times the resources each watches.

spec.title: Requests being worked on right now, by server
spec.description:
How many requests each server was working on in the last second (the server reports the maximum), reads and writes. A server that stops answering stops counting; a server under uneven load carries far more than the others.

**If not:** One server at several times the others: uneven load (429 tab). A line that ends: that server stopped reporting; see the up/down chart. All low and flat while clients report refusals: the problem is between the clients and the servers (DNS, the load balancer, the cluster network), not in the servers.

options.content:
#### Now the process log: did it restart, and why

The charts said a server was down or restarted. The server's own log (streams named `kube-apiserver-…`, not the audit stream) says why: a restart writes its startup flags and a `Caches populated` line, a crash writes a `panic`. This counts those marks per minute.

Run this in CloudWatch Logs Insights, log group `${audit_log_group}`, over the same time range. If it returns nothing, check that audit logging is turned on for the cluster before concluding nobody was there.

```
fields @timestamp, @logStream, @message
| filter @logStream like /^kube-apiserver-[^a]/
| filter @message like /flags.go:64\] FLAG|Caches populated|panic|fatal error|out of memory/
| stats count(*) as marks by bin(1m), @logStream
| sort @timestamp asc
```

Marks at the start of the window followed by a few 429s or 5xx: a planned replacement, once. Marks repeating: a crash loop; read the lines just before each one. Clients reporting `connection refused` with no marks here and no gap in the audit log: the network to the server, not the server.

spec.title: Restarts, by server
spec.description:
Each bar is one in-place restart of the API server process on that server. Requests it was handling at that moment get no answer. A replaced server shows in the up/down chart as a name that ends and a name that begins.

**If not:** One per server over a few minutes: a rolling upgrade or resize. Repeating on one server: it is crashing; the 5xx tab's resources chart and the slow tab's LIST cost chart show whether a huge LIST is the reason.

spec.title: Servers up or down
spec.description:
Whether each server answered the metrics collector: 1 is up, 0 is down. A server that is down answers nobody and leaves no request metrics, so this gap and the process log below are the evidence.

**If not:** 0 for a few minutes and a new server name appears: a planned replacement. 0 with no replacement: that server is stuck. All at 0: the metrics collector may be the problem rather than the servers; test from a client.

spec.title: Bytes per resource, the ten largest
spec.description:
How much space each resource takes, the ten largest. A resource high here but low in the objects bars is made of large objects, the kind that makes LIST and watch events slow.

**Healthy:** the same names as the objects bars, in a similar order.

**If not:** A resource far higher here than in objects: large objects (big ConfigMaps or Secrets, pods with long status); the slow tab's response size chart shows the cost.

spec.title: Objects the server could not read, by resource
spec.description:
An object in the database the server could not decode: corrupt, written by something else, or encrypted with a key that is gone (after a key rotation).

**Healthy:** none.

**If not:** Any at all: find the object (`kubectl get <resource> -A` will show the error) and the support case starts there.

spec.title: Database calls that failed, by operation and resource
spec.description:
Calls to the database that returned an error. Each one becomes a 500 for a client.

**Healthy:** none.

**If not:** The 5xx tab's database chart and log query take it from here.

spec.title: Database size against the 8 GiB limit
spec.description:
How full the database file is. EKS stops accepting writes at 8 GiB; the dial is green under half, yellow from there, red near the limit.

**Healthy:** well under half, and roughly steady.

**If not:** Climbing: the objects bars beside this say which resource is growing; a controller that creates and never deletes is the usual cause.

spec.title: Secrets encryption: KMS call time and key-cache fill
spec.description:
With KMS secrets encryption on, a Secret read or write that misses the key cache waits on a call to KMS. Lines: how long those calls take (99 in 100 under). Bars: how full the key cache is. A cold cache after a restart is a burst of KMS calls.

**Healthy:** encrypt and decrypt in tens of milliseconds; the cache fill steady.

**If not:** KMS slow or failing makes every Secret operation slow or fail: it shows up as `secrets` over its line at the top of the page.

spec.title: Objects per resource, the ten largest
spec.description:
How many objects of each resource the database holds right now, the ten largest.

**Healthy:** the resources you expect, in the proportions you expect.

**If not:** A resource you do not recognise near the top is a controller that creates and never deletes (events, jobs, leases, finished pods).

spec.title: Database size on disk
spec.description:
The size of the database file as it reports it to the API server. It grows with objects and with history; compaction frees space inside the file, and only defragmentation shrinks the file. EKS limits it to 8 GiB.

**Healthy:** a slow sawtooth: growth, then a drop at defragmentation.

**If not:** Steady growth with the objects chart flat is history not being compacted or the file not being defragmented; on EKS that is AWS's to fix. Growth with the objects chart is the objects chart's answer.

spec.title: Database call time (99 in 100 under), by operation
spec.description:
The API server's own timing of its calls to the database (etcd): get, list, create, update, delete. On EKS the database is run by AWS, so this is evidence for a support case, not something to tune.

**Healthy:** single-digit milliseconds for get and update; list in line with the size of what it lists.

**If not:** Every operation slow together: the database or the network to it. Only list slow: the objects chart says what is being listed and how big it is.

spec.title: Database call, get (slowest 1 %)
spec.description:
How long a single-object read from the database takes, the slowest 1 %, over the range.

**Healthy:** a few milliseconds.

spec.title: Database call, list (slowest 1 %)
spec.description:
How long a collection read from the database takes, the slowest 1 %, over the range.

**Healthy:** in line with the size of what is listed; under a second for most clusters.

spec.title: 5xx by code and verb
spec.description:
Errors per second by code and verb. 500 means something inside failed: a webhook did not answer, a client hung up early (the server records that as 500), or the database returned an error. 502 and 503 mean the server passed the request on to another component that was not there, such as an add-on API or a node.

**If not:** 503 on reads only: an add-on API such as metrics-server, or a node, not the API server; the resource chart names it. 500 on writes: look at the webhooks chart. 500 on everything at once: look at the database chart.

spec.expr: sum by (code, verb) (rate(apiserver_request_total{code=~"500|502|503", verb!~"WATCH|CONNECT", subresource!~"status|token|scale|/healthz|binding|proxy", verb=~"${verb_class:pipe}", resource=~"${resource:pipe}", instance=~"${instance:pipe}"}[$__rate_interval]))

options.content:
#### Now the audit log: which message

The charts said which code and which resource. The audit log says why, in words: every error carries a message. The common ones: `failed calling webhook` (a webhook, customer-owned), `error trying to reach service` (an add-on API or a node), `context canceled` (the client hung up), `etcdserver: request timed out` (the database).

Run this in CloudWatch Logs Insights, log group `${audit_log_group}`, over the same time range. If it returns nothing, check that audit logging is turned on for the cluster before concluding nobody was there.

```
fields @timestamp, verb, requestURI, user.username, responseStatus.code, responseStatus.message
| filter @logStream like /kube-apiserver-audit/ and responseStatus.code >= 500 and responseStatus.code != 504
| filter verb like /(?i)^(${verb_class:pipe})$/ and objectRef.resource like /^(${resource:pipe})$/
| stats count(*) as n by responseStatus.code, responseStatus.message, user.username
| sort n desc
| limit 50
```

The top row is your cause. Also look at `annotations.apiserver.latency.k8s.io/total` on these rows: it is only recorded for requests over 0.5 s, so blank means a quick failure; close to 60 s means they held capacity until they died.

spec.title: 5xx by resource and subresource
spec.description:
The eight resources with the most errors. The part after the slash tells you who was really answering: `nodes/proxy` and `pods/log` go to the node (`pods/exec` uses CONNECT and is left out); `pods` and `nodes` from the metrics API go to metrics-server. This chart keeps the subresources the rest of the page leaves out, so its total can exceed the 5xx tile.

**If not:** One resource has all the errors: the component behind that resource is down. Every resource at once: the API server itself or its database.

spec.expr: topk(8, sum by (resource, subresource) (rate(apiserver_request_total{code=~"500|502|503", verb!~"WATCH|CONNECT", verb=~"${verb_class:pipe}", resource=~"${resource:pipe}", instance=~"${instance:pipe}"}[$__rate_interval])))

spec.title: Restarts and servers present
spec.description:
When each server restarted in place, and how many servers are up. A restarting server drops the requests it was handling. A replaced server is not a restart: it shows as one name that stops and a new name that starts, so more names than servers in the range means an upgrade or a resize.

**If not:** One restart each, with new server names: planned, once. The same server restarting again and again: it is crashing, often from running out of memory on a huge LIST; the slow tab's LIST cost chart shows which one.

spec.title: Database calls that failed, by operation and resource
spec.description:
Calls from the API server to its database (etcd) that failed, by operation and resource. On EKS the database is managed by AWS, so this is evidence for a support case, not something to fix yourself. Each failed call is usually a 500 for the client, a 503 or 504 when the call timed out.

**If not:** Failures on every operation: the database or the network to it. Failures on one resource only: start from that resource's requests in the table at the top. No failures here while 500s climb: the database is fine; look at webhooks and clients hanging up.

spec.title: Admission webhooks: rejected, failed open, and time per call (slowest 1 %)
spec.description:
Admission webhooks are customer-run services the API server must call before it saves a write. 'Rejected' is a webhook saying no, which is its job (a webhook call that failed with failurePolicy Fail is counted here too). 'Fail-open' is a call that failed (timeout, connection error, or an error from the webhook) and was skipped because its failurePolicy is Ignore. Right axis: how long each webhook takes (slowest 1 %).

**If not:** Any fail-open is serious: a policy was silently skipped. A webhook whose time climbs to exactly its timeout while writes fail: that webhook's pods are the problem, and its name tells you whose it is.

options.content: *Prepared by Shane Corbett · Kubernetes Specialist (shancor@amazon.com). Please retain author attribution when sharing or adapting this dashboard.* · Lines: 2 s for GET and writes, 30 s for LIST (slowest 1 %), the limits this project's scanner and investigation protocol use. Audit log group: `${audit_log_group}`.

spec.title: Authentication attempts per second, by result
spec.description:
Every request is authenticated first. Success is normal. Failures and errors are a client with a bad or expired credential, usually retrying in a loop.

**Healthy:** success only; failure and error at or near zero.

**If not:** A steady band of failures is one client with a stale token or certificate: in the audit log it appears as `responseStatus.code = 401` with the username `system:anonymous`.

spec.title: Authorization webhooks: call time and fail-open
spec.description:
Some clusters ask an outside service whether a request is allowed. Lines: how long that call takes (99 in 100 under). Bars: calls the service did not answer in time, so the decision fell to the remaining authorizers (RBAC) alone (fail-open: the webhook gave no opinion), which is a permission check silently skipped.

**Healthy:** time under the dashed 0.5 s mark, no fail-open bars at all. Empty is fine on a cluster without an authorization webhook.

**If not:** Any fail-open bar: the webhook's name is its owner; its pods are down or too slow.

spec.title: Time in the request filters (99 in 100 under), by step
spec.description:
Before the server does any work on a request it checks who sent it (authentication), whether they may (authorization), records it (audit) and assigns it a priority level. Each filter has its own latency measure; `priorityandfairness` includes any time spent waiting in the queue.

**Healthy:** every step well under the dashed 0.5 s mark, flat.

**If not:** authorization high with an authorization webhook configured: the webhook chart beside this. authentication high: the token chart; a surge of cache misses means a call to the token webhook for each one. priorityandfairness high: queue wait; the fairness tab.

spec.title: Refused before handling: TLS handshake failures and audit problems
spec.description:
Requests that never became requests: connections whose TLS handshake failed (a client with a bad certificate, a load balancer health check that opens and closes a connection, or a scanner), and requests the audit layer refused or could not record. None of these are counted anywhere else on this page.

**Healthy:** all at zero.

**If not:** TLS errors in a steady band at a constant rate: usually health checks, harmless; a band that appears with a client change is a bad certificate, and the source address is in the server's own log. Audit backend errors: the audit log itself has a problem, and the log queries on this page may be missing rows.

spec.title: Token checks: cache hits and misses, and authentication time
spec.description:
The server caches the answers of the token webhook (on EKS the IAM authenticator). Lines: cache hits and misses per second. Bars: how long authentication took (99 in 100 under). A surge of misses is a surge of new tokens, each one a call to the token webhook. Service account tokens are checked inside the server and are not in this cache.

**Healthy:** mostly hits; authentication time in milliseconds.

**If not:** Misses climbing with authentication time: a client minting a new token for every request. The audit log names it.

spec.title: Authentication failures per second
spec.description:
Requests whose credentials were bad or expired, per second over the range. Usually one client retrying in a loop.

**Healthy:** 0.

**If not:** In the audit log these are `responseStatus.code = 401`; count them by source IP (`sourceIPs.0`) to find the client.

spec.title: Authorization fail-open, in the range
spec.description:
Requests on which an outside authorization service did not answer in time, so the decision fell to the remaining authorizers (RBAC) alone. Silent harm: a permission check skipped. The counter does not exist until the first event, so a cluster that has never failed open reads 'none in this range'.

**Healthy:** none in this range, or 0.

**If not:** Any: the webhook chart below names it; its pods are down or too slow.

spec.title: Slowest request filter (slowest 1 %)
spec.description:
The slowest of the request filters (authentication, authorization, audit, priority and fairness) over the range. The priority and fairness filter includes queue wait.

**Healthy:** well under the 0.5 s mark.

**If not:** Over the mark: the step chart below says which step, and the charts beside it why.

spec.title: TLS handshakes that failed, in the range
spec.description:
Connections that never got past the TLS handshake: a client with a bad certificate, a load balancer health check, or a scanner.

**Healthy:** 0 is green; a handful from health checks or scanners turns it yellow and is usual.

spec.title: The busiest kinds of request, with how slow they are
spec.description:
The 25 kinds of request with the most traffic in the range. Each row is a verb, a resource and a scope (one namespace, or the whole cluster). 'Total' is how long the slowest 1 % took; 'Server only' is the part the server spent on the work itself; '× its line' compares Total to what that kind is allowed (30 s LIST, 2 s otherwise).

**Healthy:** every '× its line' well under 1 and no colour; Total and Server only close together.

**If not:** Total far above Server only on a write: webhooks. A cluster-scoped LIST near the top of the traffic list is the usual thing to question: who needs the whole cluster that often? Click the verb or resource to focus every chart on it.

spec.expr: topk(25, sum by (verb, resource, scope) (rate(apiserver_request_duration_seconds_count{verb!~"WATCH|CONNECT", subresource!~"status|token|scale|/healthz|binding|proxy", verb=~"${verb_class:pipe}", resource=~"${resource:pipe}", instance=~"${instance:pipe}"}[$__range])))

(histogram_quantile(0.99, sum by (le, verb, resource, scope) (rate(apiserver_request_duration_seconds_bucket{verb!~"WATCH|CONNECT", subresource!~"status|token|scale|/healthz|binding|proxy", verb=~"${verb_class:pipe}", resource=~"${resource:pipe}", instance=~"${instance:pipe}", verb="LIST"}[$__range])))) and on (verb, resource, scope) (sum by (verb, resource, scope) (rate(apiserver_request_duration_seconds_count{verb!~"WATCH|CONNECT", subresource!~"status|token|scale|/healthz|binding|proxy", verb=~"${verb_class:pipe}", resource=~"${resource:pipe}", instance=~"${instance:pipe}", verb="LIST"}[$__range])) >= 0.034) or (histogram_quantile(0.99, sum by (le, verb, resource, scope) (rate(apiserver_request_duration_seconds_bucket{verb!~"WATCH|CONNECT", subresource!~"status|token|scale|/healthz|binding|proxy", verb=~"${verb_class:pipe}", resource=~"${resource:pipe}", instance=~"${instance:pipe}", verb!="LIST"}[$__range])))) and on (verb, resource, scope) (sum by (verb, resource, scope) (rate(apiserver_request_duration_seconds_count{verb!~"WATCH|CONNECT", subresource!~"status|token|scale|/healthz|binding|proxy", verb=~"${verb_class:pipe}", resource=~"${resource:pipe}", instance=~"${instance:pipe}", verb!="LIST"}[$__range])) >= 0.5)

histogram_quantile(0.99, sum by (le, verb, resource, scope) (rate(apiserver_request_sli_duration_seconds_bucket{verb!~"WATCH|CONNECT", subresource!~"status|token|scale|/healthz|binding|proxy", verb=~"${verb_class:pipe}", resource=~"${resource:pipe}", instance=~"${instance:pipe}"}[$__range])))

((histogram_quantile(0.99, sum by (le, verb, resource, scope) (rate(apiserver_request_duration_seconds_bucket{verb!~"WATCH|CONNECT", subresource!~"status|token|scale|/healthz|binding|proxy", verb=~"${verb_class:pipe}", resource=~"${resource:pipe}", instance=~"${instance:pipe}", verb="LIST"}[$__range])))) and on (verb, resource, scope) (sum by (verb, resource, scope) (rate(apiserver_request_duration_seconds_count{verb!~"WATCH|CONNECT", subresource!~"status|token|scale|/healthz|binding|proxy", verb=~"${verb_class:pipe}", resource=~"${resource:pipe}", instance=~"${instance:pipe}", verb="LIST"}[$__range])) >= 0.034)) / 30 or ((histogram_quantile(0.99, sum by (le, verb, resource, scope) (rate(apiserver_request_duration_seconds_bucket{verb!~"WATCH|CONNECT", subresource!~"status|token|scale|/healthz|binding|proxy", verb=~"${verb_class:pipe}", resource=~"${resource:pipe}", instance=~"${instance:pipe}", verb!="LIST"}[$__range])))) and on (verb, resource, scope) (sum by (verb, resource, scope) (rate(apiserver_request_duration_seconds_count{verb!~"WATCH|CONNECT", subresource!~"status|token|scale|/healthz|binding|proxy", verb=~"${verb_class:pipe}", resource=~"${resource:pipe}", instance=~"${instance:pipe}", verb!="LIST"}[$__range])) >= 0.5)) / 2

value.title: Focus every tab on this verb and resource
Focus every tab on this verb and resource

properties.value: This kind's share of the server's work.
How long the slowest 1 % took, as the client saw it.
The part the server spent on the work itself: no webhooks, no queue wait.
Total divided by what this kind is allowed (30 s LIST, 2 s otherwise). 1.0 is at the line.

spec.title: GET and writes: how long the slowest 1 % took (line at 2 s)
spec.description:
Requests that touch one object. Two measures: what the client waited, and the time the server spent on the work itself (no webhooks, no queue wait). This is the history behind the 'slow' tile for everything except LIST.

**Healthy:** both lines under the dashed 2 s line and close together.

**If not:** Both lines high: the server itself or its database (slow tab). Only the total high: the time went to webhooks or queue wait (504 tab). Read the shapes, do not subtract the lines.

spec.title: LIST: how long the slowest 1 % took (line at 30 s)
spec.description:
Requests that read a whole collection. The same two measures. The line is 30 s because a big collection may honestly take long; most should be far under it.

**Healthy:** both lines under the dashed 30 s line and close together.

**If not:** Both lines high: the server itself or its database (slow tab). Only the total high: the time went to webhooks or queue wait (504 tab). Read the shapes, do not subtract the lines.

spec.title: Answers per second, by result
spec.description:
What the server answered, not counting watch streams. 2xx is success. 4xx other than 429 is the client's mistake (not found, forbidden, conflict) and costs the server little. 429 and 5xx are the symptoms counted at the top of the page.

**Healthy:** almost all 2xx, a thin band of 4xx (a controller re-trying a conflict is normal), nothing else.

**If not:** A wide 4xx band is a client asking for things that do not exist, in a loop; the log query in any tab, filtered on `responseStatus.code = 404` or `403`, names it.

spec.title: How long every request took, over time
spec.description:
Every request in the range, placed by how long it took (up the side) and when (along the bottom). Brighter means more requests. This is the whole picture the two lines beside it summarise.

**Healthy:** one bright band near the bottom, flat across the whole range.

**If not:** A second band higher up is one kind of request that is consistently slow: the table below names it. The band lifting as a whole is the server or the database slowing down for everyone.

spec.title: Requests per second, by kind
spec.description:
How busy the API server is, split by the kind of request. LIST reads a whole collection and is the expensive one; GET and writes (including server-side APPLY) touch one object; a WATCH is a long-lived stream whose cost is per event sent, not per request, and the server counts it only when the stream ends. DELETECOLLECTION, rare, is in neither group.

**Healthy:** a steady daily rhythm you recognise. More requests is not a problem by itself.

**If not:** A step up that stays is a new client or a client that started polling. A rise in LIST with no rise in anything else is the shape that fills the server fastest; the slow tab's LIST cost chart says whether those LISTs are filtered.

spec.title: LIST share of requests
spec.description:
How much of the workload is LIST, the request that reads a whole collection and costs the most.

**Healthy:** a few percent. Controllers that watch instead of list keep this low.

**If not:** High: something is polling collections; the busiest-kinds table at the bottom names the resource.

spec.expr: 100 * sum(rate(apiserver_request_total{verb="LIST", subresource!~"status|token|scale|/healthz|binding|proxy", verb=~"${verb_class:pipe}", resource=~"${resource:pipe}", instance=~"${instance:pipe}"}[$__range])) / sum(rate(apiserver_request_total{verb!~"WATCH|CONNECT", subresource!~"status|token|scale|/healthz|binding|proxy", verb=~"${verb_class:pipe}", resource=~"${resource:pipe}", instance=~"${instance:pipe}"}[$__range]))

spec.title: Answered 2xx
spec.description:
The share of requests that succeeded.

**Healthy:** over 99 %. The rest is mostly clients asking for things that do not exist.

spec.expr: 100 * sum(rate(apiserver_request_total{code=~"2..", verb!~"WATCH|CONNECT", subresource!~"status|token|scale|/healthz|binding|proxy", verb=~"${verb_class:pipe}", resource=~"${resource:pipe}", instance=~"${instance:pipe}"}[$__range])) / sum(rate(apiserver_request_total{verb!~"WATCH|CONNECT", subresource!~"status|token|scale|/healthz|binding|proxy", verb=~"${verb_class:pipe}", resource=~"${resource:pipe}", instance=~"${instance:pipe}"}[$__range]))

spec.title: GET and writes, slowest 1 % (line 2 s)
spec.description:
How long the slowest 1 % of single-object requests took over the range.

**Healthy:** well under 2 s.

spec.title: LIST, slowest 1 % (line 30 s)
spec.description:
How long the slowest 1 % of LIST requests took over the range.

**Healthy:** well under 30 s.

spec.title: Requests per second
spec.description:
The server's workload over the range, requests per second, not counting watch streams or the housekeeping subresources (status, scale, token, binding, proxy) the whole page leaves out.

**Healthy:** whatever is normal for this cluster. A number on its own is not a verdict.

options.content: **Admission.** Before a write is saved, webhooks (customer-run services) and policies (rules inside the server) are consulted. Every webhook call adds time the server's own latency measure does not count, and a webhook that fails open is a rule silently skipped.

**Cache and watches.** The server keeps a copy of the whole cluster in memory and answers most reads from it. One stream of changes comes in from the database; thousands of watch streams go out to clients.
**The database (etcd).** You cannot see inside it on EKS, but you can see every call the server makes to it, what is stored, and how big it is.

**Authentication and authorization.** Before any work is done, a request is authenticated, authorized, audited and assigned a priority level. This is where credential problems and external authorization services show up.

**Fairness and seats.** The server sorts requests into priority levels and gives each a share of capacity, measured in seats: units of concurrency, one for an ordinary request, several for a large LIST. A full low level with a queue is priority and fairness working as designed; a full high level is not.
**The servers.** The control plane has several API servers. They should track each other: the one that diverges is carrying clients pinned to it, or is about to run out of memory.
**Traffic and speed.** How much the server is asked to do, and how fast it answers, over time. LIST is the expensive kind of request. The table at the bottom ranks the busiest kinds.

**Read this page top to bottom.** The five tiles count what clients ran into in this time range: refused (429), failed (5xx), timed out (504), slow, or no answer at all. Green means none. A coloured tile is your symptom: the chart shows when it happened, the table shows which kind of request, and the tab with the same name walks you through the usual checks and ends with a log query that names the caller. Charts say what; logs say who.

spec.title: Slowness by server (slowest 1 %): one of them, or all of them?
spec.description:
The same slowness split by server. Servers should track each other, because they serve the same cluster from the same database. The one that diverges is the one to investigate.

**If not:** One server slow with no more requests than the others: that server is busy with work these charts do not show, such as serving many watch streams (the servers tab shows them). All slow together: the database, or a request shape every server receives.

spec.title: The ladder: client → server → database (slowest 1 %), outside in
spec.description:
Four latency measures on the same requests (slowest 1 %), each one nested inside the one above: 1 is what the client waited, 2 is the server's own work, 3 is the storage layer (LIST only, and only when the LIST was not answered from the server's cache), 4 is one call to the database (every operation). The time between two rungs is the cost of the layer between them; rungs 3 and 4 nest inside 2 for LISTs, so compare them against the LIST line, not the 2 s mark.

**If not:** 1 far above 2: webhooks or the line (504 tab). 2 far above 3 and 4: the server itself, usually building a very large response or filtering a whole collection; see the LIST cost chart. 3 far above 4: the storage layer, not the database. 4 high: the database; on EKS, evidence for a support case.

options.content:
#### Now the audit log: the slowest requests and where their time went

The charts said which layer is slow. The audit log says which requests and which client: every request slower than 0.5 s records how long each stage took. `watch` and `connect` are left out because they are long-lived streams, not slow requests.

Run this in CloudWatch Logs Insights, log group `${audit_log_group}`, over the same time range. If it returns nothing, check that audit logging is turned on for the cluster before concluding nobody was there.

```
fields @timestamp, verb, requestURI, user.username, userAgent, `annotations.apiserver.latency.k8s.io/total` as total, `annotations.apiserver.latency.k8s.io/etcd` as etcd, `annotations.apiserver.latency.k8s.io/apf-queue-wait` as queue, `annotations.apiserver.latency.k8s.io/serialize-response-object` as serialize, `annotations.apiserver.latency.k8s.io/response-write` as write
| filter @logStream like /kube-apiserver-audit/ and verb not in ["watch", "connect"]
| filter verb like /(?i)^(${verb_class:pipe})$/ and objectRef.resource like /^(${resource:pipe})$/
| filter ispresent(total)
| sort @timestamp desc
| limit 100
```

A blank stage was fast. `write` close to total means a slow client reading the response, not a slow server. Then `stats count(*) by user.username, userAgent` over the same filter: the two or three names at the top are who to talk to. If the slow rows are spread over many clients through one webhook or one resource, that webhook or resource is the owner.

spec.title: LIST cost: objects the database read per object returned, by resource
spec.description:
For LISTs that went to the database: how many objects it read for each one it returned. 1 means it found exactly what was asked for. 1 000 means it read a thousand objects to return one, because the client asked for a filter the cache cannot answer. That is one of the most expensive things a client can do, and a usual cause of slow LISTs and out-of-memory restarts.

**If not:** A resource far above 1: a client is listing with a filter. The log query below names it; the fix is for the client to watch for changes instead of listing, or to list from the cache (`resourceVersion=0`).

spec.title: Response size (largest 1 %), by resource
spec.description:
How big the biggest responses are (largest 1 %), by resource. A response of hundreds of megabytes costs twice: building it, then sending it, and the server holds a seat for both.

**If not:** Large and slow together while the database is fast: the cost is building and sending the response; the client should ask for less. Large on one resource plus restarts in the 5xx tab: the server ran out of memory.

spec.expr: topk(6, histogram_quantile(0.99, sum by (le, resource) (rate(apiserver_response_sizes_bucket{verb!~"WATCH|CONNECT", subresource!~"status|token|scale|/healthz|binding|proxy", verb=~"${verb_class:pipe}", resource=~"${resource:pipe}", instance=~"${instance:pipe}"}[$__rate_interval]))))

spec.title: Seats one request was expected to cost (99 in 100 under), by priority level
spec.description:
Before a request runs, the server guesses how many seats it will need: 1 for most, more for a LIST that will return many objects or a WATCH that fans out an event. A level whose requests cost many seats each fills up with few requests.

**Healthy:** 1 on most levels; a few on levels that serve large LISTs.

**If not:** A jump here with no change in request rate means the requests changed shape: something is listing a larger collection than before.

spec.title: Busiest flows: which rule the requests matched
spec.description:
Requests per second by flow schema, the eight busiest. A flow schema is the rule that decided which priority level a request goes to (by user, group or verb). It is the closest the metrics come to naming a caller; the audit log names the user.

**Healthy:** the flows you expect on each level, in the proportions you expect.

**If not:** A busy flow on a high level you did not expect is a rule that matches too much: a caller is getting a priority it should not have.

spec.title: How full each priority level is right now
spec.description:
Priority levels each get a share of capacity, measured in seats: units of concurrency, one for an ordinary request, several for a large LIST. Each bar is one level: seats in use now over the seats it may use now, summed over the selected servers. Yellow at 70 %, red at 90 %; at 100 % requests queue.

**Healthy:** bars well short of full. A full bar on `workload-low` with a queue behind it is priority and fairness working as designed, as long as the levels above have room.

**If not:** A full bar on `system`, `node-high` or `leader-election` means the control plane is squeezing its own traffic; the table beside this shows the queue and the busiest-flows chart shows what is filling it.

spec.expr: 100 * sum by (priority_level) (apiserver_flowcontrol_current_executing_seats{priority_level=~"${priority_level:pipe}", instance=~"${instance:pipe}"}) / on (priority_level) (sum by (priority_level) (apiserver_flowcontrol_current_limit_seats{priority_level=~"${priority_level:pipe}", instance=~"${instance:pipe}"}) > 0)

spec.title: Each priority level: seats, queue, refusals, wait
spec.description:
One row per priority level: the seats it is using against its limit, the floor and ceiling of that limit, how many requests are waiting, and over the range how many were refused and how long they waited. Sorted by the queue, so a full level is on top.

**Healthy:** no one waiting and no refusals on any level; wait in milliseconds.

**If not:** A queue on `workload-low` alone is shaping, by design. A queue or refusals on `system`, `node-high` or `leader-election` is the control plane protecting itself from something that should not be there; the busiest-flows chart names it. Click a level to focus the charts on it.

properties.value: Seats held by running requests, now.
Seats this level may use now, after borrowing from and lending to other levels, summed over the selected servers.
Seats this level is always guaranteed, summed over the selected servers.
The most seats this level may borrow up to, summed over the selected servers.
Requests queued for a seat on this level, now. Any number here means the level is full.
Requests answered 429 on this level, averaged over the range.
Over the range, 9 in 10 requests waited no longer than this for a seat, counting requests refused after waiting.

value.title: Focus the fairness charts on this level

spec.title: Which level was full, and when
spec.description:
One row per priority level across the range, coloured by how full it was (seats in use over the limit, summed over the selected servers): green with room, yellow at 70 %, red at 90 %; at 100 % requests queue. The bar gauge beside this is the same thing right now, in the same colours.

**Healthy:** green rows, a short yellow stretch on `workload-low` during a job.

**If not:** A red stretch on `system`, `node-high` or `leader-election` is the control plane squeezing its own traffic at that time; open the 429 tab for the same minutes.

spec.expr: 100 * sum by (priority_level) (apiserver_flowcontrol_current_executing_seats{priority_level=~"${priority_level:pipe}", instance=~"${instance:pipe}"}) / on (priority_level) (sum by (priority_level) (apiserver_flowcontrol_current_limit_seats{priority_level=~"${priority_level:pipe}", instance=~"${instance:pipe}"}) > 0)

spec.title: Requests and 429s by server: one server, or all of them?
spec.description:
Requests and 429s per server. A client keeps one connection to one server and sends everything down it, and limits are per server, so one server can be full while the others sit idle. The requests line leaves out watch streams; the 429 line counts every verb.

**If not:** One server carries most of the requests and nearly all the 429s: uneven load, not lack of capacity. Adding servers will not help; the client should watch for changes instead of polling, and reconnecting it moves it to another server. 429s even across servers: real overload or a sizing problem.

spec.title: 429s by priority level and reason
spec.description:
The API server sorts requests into priority levels (`system`, `leader-election`, `workload-high`, `workload-low` and so on), each with its own share of capacity. Each bar is refusals per second by the level that ran out, and how: `queue-full` means refused at once, `time-out` means it waited about 15 s in line first, `concurrency-limit` means that level has no line. The chart is empty on a cluster that has never refused anything.

**If not:** One level, in sharp blocks: one client's job is too chatty; fix the client, a bigger control plane only delays the next time. Several levels at once, including `system`: the control plane itself is in trouble. Check the by-server chart first: 429s on one server while the others are idle is uneven load, not lack of capacity.

options.content:
#### Now the audit log: who was refused

The charts said which level and which server. The audit log says which client. This counts refused requests per minute per user; the user that stays at the top for the whole window is the source. A minute where many users are refused at once right after a restart is clients reconnecting, not a culprit.

Run this in CloudWatch Logs Insights, log group `${audit_log_group}`, over the same time range. If it returns nothing, check that audit logging is turned on for the cluster before concluding nobody was there.

```
fields @timestamp, user.username, userAgent, verb, objectRef.resource, responseStatus.message
| filter @logStream like /kube-apiserver-audit/ and responseStatus.code = 429
| filter verb like /(?i)^(${verb_class:pipe})$/ and objectRef.resource like /^(${resource:pipe})$/
| stats count(*) as rejected by bin(1m), user.username, @logStream
| sort rejected desc
| limit 50
```

Then see what that user does: `stats count(*) by verb, objectRef.resource, objectRef.namespace` filtered to its `user.username`. Listing every pod, secret or event in the cluster, or a tight loop of GETs, are the usual answers.

spec.title: Seats in use against the limit, by priority level
spec.description:
Capacity here is seats: units of concurrency, one for an ordinary request, several for a large LIST or a WATCH's first burst of events. Both lines are summed over the selected servers. A request holds its seats for as long as it runs, so slow requests use up seats fast. Solid line: seats in use. Dashed line: the limit now, after borrowing between levels.

**If not:** In use touching the limit while 429s happen: that level really is full, and the chart on the left says who filled it. In use well under the limit while things are slow: the server is not full, the problem is slowness; go to the slow tab.

spec.title: Queue wait (slowest 1 %) and requests queued, by priority level
spec.description:
Left axis: how long requests waited in the queue for a seat (slowest 1 %), including requests refused after waiting. Right axis, bars: how many are queued right now.

**If not:** Wait climbing toward 15 s, then 429s: the line filled and requests timed out of it; clients saw a stall, then an error. 429s with no wait at all: refused instantly; clients probably retried at once, which makes it worse, and the log query below shows who.

spec.title: Rejected · 429
spec.description:
How many requests the API server refused in this time range with HTTP 429, 'too many requests'. The server was up but full, so it told the client to try again later.

**Healthy:** 0 (green).

**If not:** Open the 429 tab. It shows which group of requests filled the server, and which client sent them.

**Shape:** a block that starts and stops sharply is one client's job running; a short spike right after a server restart is clients reconnecting and re-listing at once, and passes on its own.

spec.title: Timed out · 504
spec.description:
How many requests reached the server's request timeout (60 s by default) and were answered 504. The time went somewhere: a slow webhook, queue wait, or the database.

**Healthy:** 0.

**If not:** Open the 504 tab. It compares the two latency measures to show where the time went.

**Shape:** many requests ending at the same number of seconds point at one slow stage, often a webhook close to its own timeout (a webhook that times out is a 500, not a 504); a burst together with 429s is a full queue, because queue wait counts toward the deadline.

spec.title: Failed · 500 / 502 / 503
spec.description:
How many requests ended in a server-side error (500, 502 or 503). Most of these are not the API server itself breaking: it often relays an error from something it called, such as an admission webhook or an add-on API.

**Healthy:** 0 (green). Any error colours the tile; a handful spread thin over a quiet range is background noise, a burst is an event.

**If not:** Open the 5xx tab. It sorts the errors by code and by resource so you can see which component failed.

**Shape:** errors in the same minute as timeouts are usually one event, not two; one tight burst is an outage, a scatter is background noise.

spec.title: Not answering · restarts, servers down
spec.description:
How many times an API server process restarted in place, plus how many servers are not answering the metrics collector right now. A replaced server (new name) is not a restart here; the not answering tab shows names coming and going. A client that reaches a restarting server gets 'connection refused', and nothing else records that, so this tile is the only trace.

**Healthy:** 0. One or two, with a short blip in the other tiles, is a planned server replacement.

**If not:** Open the not answering tab. It shows which server restarted, how often, and why.

**Shape:** a single restart is a planned replacement; restarts that keep repeating are a crash loop, often from a LIST that ran the server out of memory.

spec.title: Slow · kinds over their line
spec.description:
How many kinds of request (a verb on a resource) were slower than their line at the worst moment of the range, whatever they answered. A LIST is allowed 30 s, everything else 2 s, measured on the slowest 1 % of requests. Kinds with too little traffic to judge are left out.

**Healthy:** 0.

**If not:** Open the slow tab. It follows a request from the client to the database to find where the time is spent.

**Shape:** one kind slow is one expensive request shape; everything slow at once is the server or the database; slow in sharp blocks is one client's job.

spec.expr: (count((histogram_quantile(0.99, sum by (le, verb, resource) (rate(apiserver_request_duration_seconds_bucket{subresource!~"status|token|scale|/healthz|binding|proxy", verb=~"${verb_class:pipe}", resource=~"${resource:pipe}", instance=~"${instance:pipe}", verb="LIST"}[$__rate_interval]))) > 30) and on (verb, resource) (sum by (verb, resource) (rate(apiserver_request_duration_seconds_count{subresource!~"status|token|scale|/healthz|binding|proxy", verb=~"${verb_class:pipe}", resource=~"${resource:pipe}", instance=~"${instance:pipe}", verb="LIST"}[$__rate_interval])) >= 0.034) or (histogram_quantile(0.99, sum by (le, verb, resource) (rate(apiserver_request_duration_seconds_bucket{subresource!~"status|token|scale|/healthz|binding|proxy", verb=~"${verb_class:pipe}", resource=~"${resource:pipe}", instance=~"${instance:pipe}", verb=~"GET|POST|PUT|PATCH|DELETE|APPLY"}[$__rate_interval]))) > 2) and on (verb, resource) (sum by (verb, resource) (rate(apiserver_request_duration_seconds_count{subresource!~"status|token|scale|/healthz|binding|proxy", verb=~"${verb_class:pipe}", resource=~"${resource:pipe}", instance=~"${instance:pipe}", verb=~"GET|POST|PUT|PATCH|DELETE|APPLY"}[$__rate_interval])) >= 0.5))) or vector(0)

spec.title: When: every symptom, minute by minute
spec.description:
The same five counts, minute by minute, so you can see when things happened and whether they happened together.

**Healthy:** flat lines at zero.

**If not:** Lines that spike together in one minute, with a restart, are one server being replaced. A flat-topped block is one client's job. A slow rise with no restart is growing load. Open the tab of the line that leads.

spec.expr: (count((histogram_quantile(0.99, sum by (le, verb, resource) (rate(apiserver_request_duration_seconds_bucket{subresource!~"status|token|scale|/healthz|binding|proxy", verb=~"${verb_class:pipe}", resource=~"${resource:pipe}", instance=~"${instance:pipe}", verb="LIST"}[$__rate_interval]))) > 30) and on (verb, resource) (sum by (verb, resource) (rate(apiserver_request_duration_seconds_count{subresource!~"status|token|scale|/healthz|binding|proxy", verb=~"${verb_class:pipe}", resource=~"${resource:pipe}", instance=~"${instance:pipe}", verb="LIST"}[$__rate_interval])) >= 0.034) or (histogram_quantile(0.99, sum by (le, verb, resource) (rate(apiserver_request_duration_seconds_bucket{subresource!~"status|token|scale|/healthz|binding|proxy", verb=~"${verb_class:pipe}", resource=~"${resource:pipe}", instance=~"${instance:pipe}", verb=~"GET|POST|PUT|PATCH|DELETE|APPLY"}[$__rate_interval]))) > 2) and on (verb, resource) (sum by (verb, resource) (rate(apiserver_request_duration_seconds_count{subresource!~"status|token|scale|/healthz|binding|proxy", verb=~"${verb_class:pipe}", resource=~"${resource:pipe}", instance=~"${instance:pipe}", verb=~"GET|POST|PUT|PATCH|DELETE|APPLY"}[$__rate_interval])) >= 0.5))) or vector(0)

spec.title: Time the client waited vs time the server worked (slowest 1 %)
spec.description:
Two latency measures on the same requests (slowest 1 %). 'Total' is what the client waited. 'SLI' is only the time the server spent on the work itself; it leaves out calling webhooks and queue wait. The gap between the two lines is time spent outside the server.

**If not:** Total far above SLI: the time went to a webhook or the queue; the two charts below say which. Both high and close together: the server or its database; go to the slow tab.

options.content:
#### Now the audit log: which stage ate the deadline

The charts said whether the time went to webhooks, the line or the server. The audit log says it per request: every slow request records how long each stage took. Compare each stage column to `total`.

Run this in CloudWatch Logs Insights, log group `${audit_log_group}`, over the same time range. If it returns nothing, check that audit logging is turned on for the cluster before concluding nobody was there.

```
fields @timestamp, verb, requestURI, user.username, `annotations.apiserver.latency.k8s.io/total` as total, `annotations.apiserver.latency.k8s.io/apf-queue-wait` as queue, `annotations.apiserver.latency.k8s.io/etcd` as etcd, `annotations.apiserver.latency.k8s.io/mutating-webhook` as mutating, `annotations.apiserver.latency.k8s.io/validating-webhook` as validating, `annotations.apiserver.latency.k8s.io/response-write` as write
| filter @logStream like /kube-apiserver-audit/ and responseStatus.code = 504
| filter verb like /(?i)^(${verb_class:pipe})$/ and objectRef.resource like /^(${resource:pipe})$/
| sort @timestamp desc
| limit 50
```

`queue` close to total: the request waited for a seat (429 tab). A webhook column close to total: that webhook. `etcd` close to total: the database. Every stage small but total at the deadline: the client gave up, or the time is in a stage not listed here. Values are text like `30.9s` or `1m0.0s`; read them as durations.

spec.title: Requests the server terminated, by code and resource
spec.description:
Requests the server cut off itself, in self-defence, instead of finishing. 504 is the deadline; 429 is a refusal by priority and fairness or the in-flight limit (the 429 tab); other codes are a server shutting down. Split by resource so one slow resource stands out.

**If not:** 504 on one resource: an expensive request shape, such as a filtered LIST over a large collection. 504 on every resource: the server was restarting (see the 5xx tab) or the database stalled. 429 here repeats the 429 tab.

spec.title: Queue wait before running (slowest 1 %), by priority level
spec.description:
How long requests waited in the queue for a seat (slowest 1 %), per priority level, including requests refused after waiting. A request that waits too long in the queue is refused with a 429 (reason `time-out`), not a 504; but wait that does not time out still counts toward the 60 s deadline, so a full queue turns slow requests into 504s.

**If not:** Wait climbing in one level: that level is full; the 429 tab says whether it is one client or one hot server. Wait flat while 504s climb: not the line; look at webhooks or the database.

spec.title: Webhook time per call (slowest 1 %), by webhook
spec.description:
How long each admission webhook takes (slowest 1 %), the six slowest. The server waits at most 10 s for a webhook by default, up to 30 s if configured. A webhook stuck at exactly that number is not slow, it is not answering: the write ends in a 500 (failurePolicy Fail) or goes on without it (Ignore, fail-open), and either way every write it covers waits the full time first.

**If not:** A flat line at 10 s or 30 s: that webhook's pods are down or overloaded; `kubectl get endpoints` on its service, and its name tells you whose it is. A webhook that gets slower as traffic grows needs more replicas.

spec.title: CPU per server (cores)
spec.description:
CPU used by each API server process, in cores. A busy server is allowed; what matters is whether the servers are busy together.

**Healthy:** servers track each other.

**If not:** One server hot and the others not: it is carrying the load (the requests chart beside this). Building large responses and serving many watches are the usual CPU costs.

spec.title: CPU per server, right now (cores)
spec.description:
One bar per API server: CPU in use right now, in cores. The bars should be about the same length.

**Healthy:** bars about equal.

**If not:** One bar much longer: that server is doing the work; the in-flight chart below shows whether it also has the most clients.

spec.title: Deprecated APIs still being called
spec.description:
Every deprecated API that has received a request since the server process started (the metric is not limited to the time range), with the Kubernetes release that removes it. Each row is a client that will break at that upgrade.

**Healthy:** an empty table.

**If not:** Find the caller now, not after the upgrade: in CloudWatch Logs Insights, filter the audit log on `requestURI like /^\/apis\/<group>\/<version>\//` (core group: `/^\/api\/v1\//`) and count by `user.username`.

defaults.noValue: No deprecated API has been called since the servers started

spec.title: Requests being worked on and long-running requests open, by server
spec.description:
How many requests each server was working on in the last second, and how many long-running requests (watch streams, and the rare exec or proxy) it holds open. A client keeps one connection to one server and sends everything down it, so the servers are not always even.

**Healthy:** servers track each other.

**If not:** One server with far more than the others: its clients are pinned to it. Replacing the servers spreads them out; more servers will not. The 429 tab's by-server chart shows whether that server is also refusing.

spec.title: Memory per server, and the gap between them
spec.description:
Memory used by each API server process. Most of it is the in-memory copy of the cluster and the responses being built, so it grows with the number of objects and with large LISTs. A server that runs out is restarted.

**Healthy:** servers within a few hundred megabytes of each other, and flat; the gap tile above turns yellow at a gigabyte.

**If not:** One server apart: the clients pinned to it (the requests chart beside this). All rising together: the database tab's objects chart. Rising then dropping to zero and starting again: an out-of-memory restart; see the not answering tab.

spec.expr: max(process_resident_memory_bytes{instance=~"${instance:pipe}"} and on (instance) sum by (instance) (apiserver_request_total)) - min(process_resident_memory_bytes{instance=~"${instance:pipe}"} and on (instance) sum by (instance) (apiserver_request_total))

spec.title: Memory per server, right now
spec.description:
One bar per API server: memory in use right now. The bars should be about the same length.

**Healthy:** bars within a few hundred megabytes of each other.

**If not:** One bar much longer: that server carries the clients pinned to it, or is heading for an out-of-memory restart; the history chart below says which.

spec.title: Memory gap, largest minus smallest
spec.description:
How far apart the servers are in memory. The servers serve the same cluster from the same database and should be close.

**Healthy:** under a gigabyte; a few hundred megabytes is usual.

**If not:** Over: one server is carrying more; the bars beside this say which.

spec.expr: max(process_resident_memory_bytes{instance=~"${instance:pipe}"} and on (instance) sum by (instance) (apiserver_request_total)) - min(process_resident_memory_bytes{instance=~"${instance:pipe}"} and on (instance) sum by (instance) (apiserver_request_total))

spec.title: Which kind of request: rows with a symptom
spec.description:
Which kinds of request had a problem. Each row is a verb (what was done) and a resource (what it was done to), with how many requests there were, how many got each error, and how long the slowest 1 % took (p99). '× its line' compares that to what the kind is allowed, 30 s for LIST and 2 s for everything else, so 1.0 is right at the line. A rare kind of request still gets its row: it may be the only thing one client does.

**Healthy:** an empty table (Grafana says 'No data'). 'too few' means too little traffic to judge speed.

**If not:** Click a verb or resource to focus every tab on that kind of request, then open the tab of the coloured column. The table says what kind of request; the caller's name comes from the log query at the end of each tab.

spec.expr: sum by (verb, resource) (increase(apiserver_request_total{verb!~"WATCH|CONNECT", subresource!~"status|token|scale|/healthz|binding|proxy", verb=~"${verb_class:pipe}", resource=~"${resource:pipe}", instance=~"${instance:pipe}"}[$__range]))

sum by (verb, resource) (increase(apiserver_request_total{code="429", subresource!~"status|token|scale|/healthz|binding|proxy", verb=~"${verb_class:pipe}", resource=~"${resource:pipe}", instance=~"${instance:pipe}"}[$__range]))

sum by (verb, resource) (increase(apiserver_request_total{code=~"500|502|503", verb!~"WATCH|CONNECT", subresource!~"status|token|scale|/healthz|binding|proxy", verb=~"${verb_class:pipe}", resource=~"${resource:pipe}", instance=~"${instance:pipe}"}[$__range]))

sum by (verb, resource) (increase(apiserver_request_total{code="504", subresource!~"status|token|scale|/healthz|binding|proxy", verb=~"${verb_class:pipe}", resource=~"${resource:pipe}", instance=~"${instance:pipe}"}[$__range]))

(histogram_quantile(0.99, sum by (le, verb, resource) (rate(apiserver_request_duration_seconds_bucket{subresource!~"status|token|scale|/healthz|binding|proxy", verb=~"${verb_class:pipe}", resource=~"${resource:pipe}", instance=~"${instance:pipe}", verb="LIST"}[$__range])))) and on (verb, resource) (sum by (verb, resource) (rate(apiserver_request_duration_seconds_count{subresource!~"status|token|scale|/healthz|binding|proxy", verb=~"${verb_class:pipe}", resource=~"${resource:pipe}", instance=~"${instance:pipe}", verb="LIST"}[$__range])) >= 0.034) or (histogram_quantile(0.99, sum by (le, verb, resource) (rate(apiserver_request_duration_seconds_bucket{subresource!~"status|token|scale|/healthz|binding|proxy", verb=~"${verb_class:pipe}", resource=~"${resource:pipe}", instance=~"${instance:pipe}", verb=~"GET|POST|PUT|PATCH|DELETE|APPLY"}[$__range])))) and on (verb, resource) (sum by (verb, resource) (rate(apiserver_request_duration_seconds_count{subresource!~"status|token|scale|/healthz|binding|proxy", verb=~"${verb_class:pipe}", resource=~"${resource:pipe}", instance=~"${instance:pipe}", verb=~"GET|POST|PUT|PATCH|DELETE|APPLY"}[$__range])) >= 0.5)

((histogram_quantile(0.99, sum by (le, verb, resource) (rate(apiserver_request_duration_seconds_bucket{subresource!~"status|token|scale|/healthz|binding|proxy", verb=~"${verb_class:pipe}", resource=~"${resource:pipe}", instance=~"${instance:pipe}", verb="LIST"}[$__range])))) and on (verb, resource) (sum by (verb, resource) (rate(apiserver_request_duration_seconds_count{subresource!~"status|token|scale|/healthz|binding|proxy", verb=~"${verb_class:pipe}", resource=~"${resource:pipe}", instance=~"${instance:pipe}", verb="LIST"}[$__range])) >= 0.034)) / 30 or ((histogram_quantile(0.99, sum by (le, verb, resource) (rate(apiserver_request_duration_seconds_bucket{subresource!~"status|token|scale|/healthz|binding|proxy", verb=~"${verb_class:pipe}", resource=~"${resource:pipe}", instance=~"${instance:pipe}", verb=~"GET|POST|PUT|PATCH|DELETE|APPLY"}[$__range])))) and on (verb, resource) (sum by (verb, resource) (rate(apiserver_request_duration_seconds_count{subresource!~"status|token|scale|/healthz|binding|proxy", verb=~"${verb_class:pipe}", resource=~"${resource:pipe}", instance=~"${instance:pipe}", verb=~"GET|POST|PUT|PATCH|DELETE|APPLY"}[$__range])) >= 0.5)) / 2

spec.name: datasource
spec.label: Data source
spec.description: The Prometheus-type data source holding the cluster's metrics (Amazon Managed Service for Prometheus or Prometheus).

spec.name: verb_class
spec.query: LIST : LIST, CRUD : GET|POST|PUT|PATCH|DELETE|APPLY, WATCH : WATCH
spec.label: Verb class
spec.description: Narrow to LIST, CRUD (GET and writes) or WATCH. A LIST is allowed 30 s, a GET 2 s. Clicking a row in the table sets this to that row's verb.

spec.name: resource
spec.label: Resource
spec.description: Focus every tab on one resource. Set by clicking a row in the table.

spec.name: instance
spec.label: Instance
spec.description: Focus on one API server; the by-server charts always show all of them.

spec.name: priority_level
spec.label: Priority level
spec.description: Focus the seats and queue charts on one priority level (a group of requests with its own share of capacity).

spec.name: audit_log_group
spec.label: Audit log group
spec.description: The CloudWatch log group the cluster's control-plane logs go to (/aws/eks/<cluster>/cluster); used by the log query at the end of every tab.
